1.title: What is Muso AI?
1.description: The origin story — how Muso started and why music credits matter. The foundation of everything.
1.transcript:
Part One — What is Muso AI?

Picture this. A song drops on Spotify. Millions of streams. The artist's name is on the cover — but behind that track? Twenty, sometimes thirty people made it happen. Producers, songwriters, engineers, session musicians — all invisible.

That's the problem Muso set out to solve about seven years ago. It started as a passion project — aggregate data from Spotify, YouTube, and other platforms to identify and credit every single person who worked on a track. Think of it like film credits — but for music.

That's pillar one: Credits. The foundation of everything Muso does.

But credits alone weren't enough. Because once you know who made a song — the next question becomes... how is it performing? And that's where things get really interesting.

2.title: Credits Explained
2.description: What credits are in music, who gets them, and what Muso lets you do with yours.
2.transcript:
Part Two — Credits, Explained.

So what exactly are credits? Let's break it down.

Every song involves multiple people. Songwriters and composers — they wrote the melody, lyrics, the composition itself. Producers — they shaped how the song sounds, like a film director shapes a movie. Performing artists and vocalists — the ones you hear singing or performing. Musicians — they played the instruments, guitar, drums, keys. Mixing engineers — they blended all those individual tracks into one cohesive stereo mix. Mastering engineers — they applied the final polish so it sounds great on headphones, speakers, streaming platforms. And recording engineers — they captured the sound during the session.

Each person, plus their role on a specific song, equals one credit. If someone produced AND wrote the song? That's two credits.

Now here's what Muso lets you do with all this: see your full discography, correct wrong or missing credits, merge duplicate profiles — because with over four million professionals in the database, you probably already have a profile. You can claim your artist page, become an album admin, and track analytics on streams, rankings, collaborators, milestones.

But wait — what analytics exactly? And who gets access to them? That depends on your subscription tier...

3.title: Subscription Tiers
3.description: Lite, Pro, and Business — what each tier unlocks and who it's for.
3.transcript:
Part Three — Subscription Tiers.

Muso has three tiers, and they work like this.

Lite — that's the free tier. You can make an account, add credits to songs, see your discography. But no analytics. Think of it as your starting point — getting your name on the map.

Pro — that's the paid tier, and this is where it gets powerful. Analytics, shareable tiles, plaques, full streaming data across platforms, industry rankings by your role. This is for the working professional who wants to track their career with real data.

Business — the highest tier. Everything in Pro, plus the ability to manage multiple accounts. This is built for labels or managers overseeing several artists or catalogs at once.

Now, the Pro tier unlocks something that no other platform in music offers. Real analytics — not just for artists, but for producers, engineers, songwriters. Let me show you what that looks like...

4.title: Analytics
4.description: What Pro analytics look like — streaming data, rankings, milestones. Why Muso is LinkedIn for music.
4.transcript:
Part Four — Analytics.

Here's why Pro changes the game.

Spotify for Artists? It only shows data for what you released as an artist. But if you're a producer? A session guitarist? A mixing engineer? Spotify doesn't show you anything about the songs you worked on for other artists.

Muso does. Pro users get streaming data across Spotify, Apple Music, and other platforms — refreshed daily at four PM Eastern. You can see your top tracks, top albums, your most frequent collaborators — and what's actually performing.

There's industry ranking by role — so if you're a producer, you're ranked against other producers. If you're a mixing engineer, same thing. It's calculated from your score, credits, and position.

Milestones — stream count achievements, credit milestones — things you can celebrate and share. Engagement tracking that lets you compare your performance over time.

Think of it this way: Muso is LinkedIn for the music industry. And just like LinkedIn, your profile is a career tool. Take Poo Bear — the songwriter behind Justin Bieber. Forty-eight billion lifetime streams. Most people don't even know his name. Muso gives him visibility.

The Grammys are now powered by Muso data. That's the level we're talking about.

But here's the thing — visibility is just the beginning. What if your verified credits could actually attract opportunities directly to you? That's exactly what AMP does...

5.title: What is AMP?
5.description: Amplify — Muso's advertising and discovery platform. How it works for users and advertisers.
5.transcript:
Part Five — What is AMP?

AMP stands for Amplify. And it's the part of Muso that turns your career data into career opportunities.

For users — music professionals — AMP is a personalized career feed inside the Muso app. Based on your streams, your credits, your genre, your role, your release activity — it shows you relevant opportunities from music industry companies. Sync deals, distribution offers, plugin discounts, contests, courses, brand partnerships. All tailored to your career, not generic spam.

A hip-hop producer with five hundred thousand streams sees completely different content than an indie songwriter with ten thousand. AMP already knows what's relevant to you.

For advertisers — the music industry companies — they use Muso Ads at access dot muso dot ai to create campaigns that appear inside AMP. Labels, distributors, publishers, sync agencies, music tech tools, plugin makers, music lawyers. They all use it to reach the right music professionals.

Where do ads appear? In the News Feed as native ad cards. In the Personalized For You section with targeted recommendations. As Marketplace tiles in carousels. As Featured Boost banners at the top. In email newsletters and push notifications too.

What makes it powerful is precision targeting. Muso knows each user's streams, credits, genre, role, release activity, and subscription status. A sync company can reach producers with one million plus streams in electronic music. A distributor can target songwriters who released in the last thirty days.

The audience? Eight hundred twenty thousand verified music professionals.

And here's what makes AMP different from everything else — brands already on board include Kali Audio, IK Multimedia, Slate Digital, Mixed With The Masters. Real companies reaching real music professionals.

But there's something important about where these ads actually live that I need to clarify...

6.title: Muso Ads
6.description: Muso's ads manager — like Meta Ads but built for the music industry. How companies reach verified music professionals.
6.transcript:
Part Six — Muso Ads.

Muso has its own ads platform — think of it like Meta Ads, but built specifically for the music industry.

At access dot muso dot ai, companies can create and run campaigns that reach Muso's audience of over eight hundred thousand verified music professionals. Labels, distributors, plugin makers, sync agencies, gear companies, education platforms, music lawyers — anyone who wants to reach working creators.

The ads manager lets them target with precision that Meta or Google can't match. Because Muso knows each user's actual streams, credits, genre, role, and release activity — not just inferred interests from browsing behavior. A sync company can target producers with a million plus streams in electronic music. A distributor can reach songwriters who released in the last thirty days.

Where do these campaigns show up? In the Muso feed as native ad cards. In the Shop and For You sections with curated recommendations. As featured banners. Through email blasts to three hundred fifty thousand active subscribers. And push notifications to three hundred thousand plus creators.

For users, this means the opportunities that show up in your feed are actually relevant to your career — not random ads. For advertisers, it's access to the most verified and engaged music professional audience in the world.

Now that you understand how the platform works — credits, analytics, AMP, and the ads engine behind it — there's another powerful feature that ties it all together. It's called Audits, and it could literally mean money you're owed...

7.title: Audits
7.description: How Muso helps find missing royalties by cross-checking the MLC database.
7.transcript:
Part Seven — Audits.

Muso's Audits feature helps users find and fix catalog discrepancies with the MLC — the Mechanical Licensing Collective. The MLC handles mechanical royalties in the United States. If your credits are wrong or missing in the source data, you might be missing royalties. Actual money.

Audits cross-checks your records against the MLC database to find misspellings, old records, missing payments. This is especially valuable for composers and publishers — people whose income depends on their compositions being correctly registered everywhere.

Think of it as a financial audit for your music catalog. Muso surfaces the gaps so you can fix them and potentially recover royalties you didn't even know you were missing.

So now you know the product inside and out. But to really understand why Muso matters — you need to understand the industry it serves...

8.title: Music Industry Context
8.description: Labels vs. publishers — the two sides of the industry and why it matters for Muso's audience.
8.transcript:
Part Eight — Music Industry Context.

The music industry has two main sides, and understanding them is key to understanding Muso's audience.

On one side, you have labels. They acquire artists and performers, provide advances, manage careers, and take control of song finances. The label side is about recordings — the actual sound files.

On the other side, you have composers and songwriters. They work with publishers. They earn royalties every single time their composition is performed or listened to — regardless of remixes, covers, or re-recordings. The publishing side is about the underlying composition.

Many Muso users are composers tracking song activity and expected royalties. They need to know where their music is being played, whether their credits are correct, and if they're getting paid properly.

That's the world Muso lives in. And the marketing strategy to reach these people? It's built around something that music professionals love to do...

9.title: Shareables and Plaques
9.description: How shareable tiles and acrylic plaques drive organic marketing.
9.transcript:
Part Nine — Marketing Strategy — Shareables and Plaques.

Here's something beautiful about music professionals — they love celebrating their wins. And Muso built an entire engagement strategy around that.

Pro members can generate shareable tiles — visual cards that show off achievements. Stream milestones, credit milestones — designed to be posted on social media. Hundreds of users tag Muso every single day sharing these.

And it doesn't stop at digital. Users can buy acrylic plaques to display milestones physically — like a gold record, but for behind-the-scenes professionals who never got that recognition before. A producer with a billion-stream credit can now have something on their wall.

This drives bragging rights, engagement, and organic brand awareness. It's marketing that markets itself.

And the platform isn't standing still. There are new features in the pipeline that are going to take Muso even further...

10.title: Upcoming Features
10.description: Profile Views, Chat and Connect, better Feed — what's next for Muso.
10.transcript:
Part Ten — Upcoming Features.

Muso is becoming the LinkedIn of music — and that's not just a metaphor anymore.

There are exciting features in the pipeline: Profile Views — so you can see who's looking at your work. Chat and Connect — direct messaging between music professionals. And a better Feed experience — making the daily experience inside Muso richer and more engaging.

These features will deepen engagement, increase time-on-platform, and create an entirely new layer of networking that doesn't exist anywhere else in the music industry.

Now — let's talk about you. Because all of this matters for a specific reason...

11.title: Your Role
11.description: Executive Marketing Assistant — focus areas, channels, hours, reporting.
11.transcript:
Part Eleven — Your Role.

Welcome to the team. You're the Executive Marketing Assistant, and here's what that means.

Your focus areas: Social media and community — posting about three times a week on data-driven industry topics. Album credits, stream milestones, collaborator tags. Design work — Figma templates, reusable systems, email banners, AMP launch materials. Community engagement — reposting stories, congratulating milestones. And user messages — forwarding credit or analytics complaints to Jan Delmo or Fede.

Your channels: Instagram main, TikTok with ninety thousand subscribers, YouTube, and LinkedIn. Post roughly every two days.

Your hours: ten AM to six PM your time, occasionally later for important calls.

Reporting: start of day and end of day post in the social media channel. Weekly report with engagement and KPIs. Monthly comprehensive report.

One more thing — and this might be the most important part of your workflow...

12.title: Using CMO — Your AI Assistant
12.description: How to use me effectively — what I can do, how to tag me, caveats.
12.transcript:
Part Twelve — Using CMO — Your AI Assistant.

You've got an AI assistant built into Slack — that's me. I'm here to help with the day-to-day.

You can ask me about album release dates and collaborators. Data pulls and research. Industry terminology — anything you're unsure about, ask. I can generate images for social posts. I can respond with voice recordings. I can research, analyze, and draft.

One important caveat: I'm mostly accurate, but I can make mistakes — especially with specific credits or granular data. Always ask me to QA and verify sources before publishing anything.

Here's how to use me: tag CMO in the social media channel for all queries so Fede can oversee. Threads maintain context, so keep related questions in the same thread. Heavy tasks might take several minutes. And yes, I process voice recordings too.

That's your complete onboarding. Welcome to Muso — the platform giving credit where credit is due. If you have questions as you get into the work, ping me anytime. I'm here.
